title: What are Financial Ratios?
subtitle: Why you need ratios to compare businesses
openingQuestion: Company A earns 100 billion in profit, Company B earns 10 billion. Is A better than B?
openingOptions: No, B is smaller so it's better
You can't tell yet - you need to know capital, assets, and revenue to compare
explanation: An absolute number doesn't tell you whether a business is performing well or poorly, because it says nothing about the scale of resources spent to get there. 100 billion of profit on 2,000 billion of capital (ROE 5%) is worse than 10 billion of profit on 100 billion of capital (ROE 10%), even though the first figure is ten times larger. A ratio does exactly one thing: it divides the result by the resource, so a large company and a small one stand on the same yardstick. That's also why every comparison only makes sense within the same industry - each industry has its own benchmark.

realWorldExample.description: Vietcombank posts tens of trillions of dong in absolute profit each year, dwarfing a phone retail chain many times over - but a direct comparison is nearly meaningless because their capital and asset scale are entirely different; only ROE and ROA allow a fair comparison.

quiz.question: When using ratios to compare, what's the most important thing to keep in mind?
options: Pick the ratio with the highest value
Compare within the same industry and the same period
Use as many ratios as possible and then average them
Prioritise the most recent quarter's figures since they reflect the present
quiz.explanation: A ratio only means something in context: same industry (a 20% gross margin is good for a retailer but bad for a pharma company), same period, and against that same company's own history.

quiz.question: Why is 'absolute profit' one of the most misleading numbers when comparing two businesses?
options: Because accounting standards recognise revenue differently across countries
Because an absolute number is always rounded
Because it doesn't say how much capital was used to produce it
Because absolute profit hasn't had tax subtracted yet, so it can't be compared
quiz.explanation: Ratios exist precisely to solve this problem - normalising profit against the capital/assets/revenue spent, allowing a genuine efficiency comparison between businesses of very different scale.

quiz.question: Company A earns 100 billion on 2,000 billion of equity; Company B earns 10 billion on 100 billion of equity. Who uses capital more efficiently?
options: They're equal, since the profit-to-revenue ratio is the same
A, since its profit is ten times larger than B's
A, since a larger capital base makes it safer
B, since its ROE reaches 10% versus A's 5%
quiz.explanation: A earns 10 times more than B in absolute terms but uses 20 times more capital. A's ROE is 100/2,000 = 5%, B's is 10/100 = 10% - B generates twice the profit per dong of shareholder capital invested.

quiz.question: Which metric normalises profit against assets rather than equity?
options: ROA - return on total assets
ROE - return on equity
Gross Margin - gross profit over revenue
Asset Turnover - revenue over total assets
quiz.explanation: Each ratio group picks a different denominator. ROA uses total assets, ROE uses equity, margin uses revenue. Asset Turnover also divides by assets, but its numerator is revenue, not profit.

quiz.question: A business has an ROE of 18%, above the industry average of 12%. What's the most reasonable conclusion?
options: The business clearly has a durable, sustainable competitive advantage over its rivals
You need to check the multi-year trend and debt structure before concluding anything
You should buy the stock since ROE beats the industry average
The industry is declining, which is pulling the average down
quiz.explanation: A single number at a single point in time doesn't say much yet. An 18% ROE could come from real efficiency, from high leverage, or from a one-off gain during the period - three different causes leading to three very different investment conclusions.

keyTakeaways: Ratios normalise data for a fair comparison
Compare within the same industry and the same period
Combining several ratios gives a fuller picture

practicePrompt.question: Company A has revenue of 10,000 billion and profit of 500 billion; Company B has revenue of 200 billion and profit of 30 billion. Looking only at absolute profit, A looks 'more efficient' than B. Using a ratio (Net Margin = Profit/Revenue) to compare instead, what do you find?
options: A is always more efficient than B because its absolute profit is much larger - a ratio can't change that
A's Net Margin is 5% against B's 15% - B is the more efficient one despite being smaller
These two companies can't be compared at all because they operate at very different revenue scales
A ratio only makes sense when comparing companies with the same absolute revenue scale
practicePrompt.explanation: Ratios normalise data for a fair comparison: A has a Net Margin of 500/10,000 = 5%, B has 30/200 = 15%. Even though A earns more in absolute profit, B is converting revenue into profit three times more efficiently - which is why investors always use ratios rather than looking at absolute numbers alone.

summary.keyIdea: Ratios normalise data for a fair comparison
summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Compare within the same industry and the same period

application.title: Compare two companies in the same industry
application.message: Pick two companies in the same industry with different capital scales, calculate ROE for both, and check whether the smaller one is really less efficient.
application.secondary: Absolute numbers are easy to be misled by - a ratio gives you the fair picture.

sections.text: Looking only at absolute numbers, Vietcombank earning tens of trillions of dong per year looks like an absolute 'winner' next to a phone retail chain earning a few hundred billion - but that comparison is nearly meaningless. Financial ratios exist to answer a much fairer question: for every dong of capital, every dong of assets, every dong of revenue spent, how much profit does the business generate?

Say Company A has 2,000 billion of equity and earns 100 billion/year, while Company B has 100 billion of equity and earns 10 billion/year. Looking at absolute numbers, A earns 10 times more than B. But calculating ROE (Return on Equity): A reaches 100/2,000 = 5%, while B reaches 10/100 = 10% - B is using capital twice as efficiently as A. This is why professional investors almost never compare absolute profit between two companies of different scale.

Each ratio group normalises profit (or another metric) against a different denominator: revenue (margin ratios), assets (ROA, Asset Turnover), equity (ROE), or invested capital (ROIC). Picking the right denominator for a comparison is a skill just as important as calculating the formula correctly - comparing a bank's ROE with a manufacturer's ROA is a mismatched comparison from the start.

sections.label: The golden rule when using ratios
sections.text: Only compare ratios within the same industry, the same period, and ideally by tracking that same company's own trend over several years - a single ratio at a single point in time rarely tells the whole story.

items: Only meaningful within the same industry: a 20% gross margin is good for a retailer but poor for a pharma company
Same period: comparing Q4 (peak season) with Q2 (off-season) will distort the comparison
The trend over time matters more than a number at a single point in time
No single ratio is 'the only metric you need to know' - always combine several different ratio groups

lines: Ratios don't replace reading financial statements - they're just a tool that makes comparison fairer.
The next 20 lessons go through each of the most important ratio groups every investor needs to know.
